sections.heading: Festivals and traditions
sections.body:
- *el Día de Muertos* (Mexico, Nov 1–2): families honor their dead with *altares*, *ofrendas* (offerings), *calaveras de azúcar* (sugar skulls) and *pan de muerto*.
- *el Carnaval* (before Lent): huge in Barranquilla (Colombia), Oruro (Bolivia), Montevideo.
- *la Semana Santa* (Holy Week), *la Navidad*, *la Nochebuena* (Christmas Eve), *el Año Nuevo* — in many countries you eat *doce uvas* (twelve grapes) at midnight.
- *las posadas* (Mexico, Dec 16–24), *la quinceañera* (a girl's 15th-birthday celebration), *el Inti Raymi* (Festival of the Sun, Cusco, June).
- *la fiesta patronal* (a town's patron saint festival), *los fuegos artificiales* (fireworks), *el desfile* (parade), *disfrazarse* (to dress up in costume).

sections.heading: Vosotros: Spain's "you all"
sections.body:
In Spain, *vosotros / vosotras* is the informal plural "you"; *ustedes* is only formal there. You'll hear it in Spanish films and series, so learn to **recognise** it (you don't need to use it):

- Present: *habláis, coméis, vivís, sois, estáis, tenéis, vais*
- Preterite: *hablasteis, comisteis*
- Commands: *¡Hablad! ¡Venid! ¡Sentaos!*
- Pronouns: *os* (you all, object) and *vuestro / vuestra* (your): *Os quiero. ¿Es vuestra casa?*

sections.heading: Voseo: vos instead of tú
sections.body:
In Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and much of Central America, people use *vos* instead of *tú*, with its own verb forms (stress on the last syllable): *vos hablás, vos comés, vos vivís, vos sos* (you are), *vos tenés, vos querés, vos podés*. Commands: *¡Hablá! ¡Vení! ¡Decime!* Pronouns stay *te* and *tu*: *Vos te llamás Ana, ¿no? ¿Es tu casa?*

In Colombia and parts of Central America, *vos* is also common in some regions. It's warm and informal — understand it; use it if you live there.
